title: Research Bite #40: Those Who Understand: Knowledge Growth in Teaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #40 revisits Lee S. Shulman's landmark paper 'Those Who Understand: Knowledge Growth in Teaching,' which confronts the old put-down that 'those who can't, teach' by arguing that teaching is actually the ultimate demonstration of understanding. Shulman's central move is diagnosing a 'missing paradigm' in teacher-effectiveness research: decades of process-product studies had reduced good teaching to generic, content-free behaviors, while ignoring what teachers actually need to know about their subject matter. In response, he proposes three categories of teacher knowledge — subject matter content knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, and curricular knowledge — with pedagogical content knowledge (the blend of subject and pedagogy that makes a topic teachable) doing the most work. He further distinguishes propositional knowledge, case knowledge, and strategic knowledge, arguing that true professional judgment is developed through the dialectic application of principles and specific cases. Barton's framing for teachers is that expertise isn't just knowing your subject or knowing generic teaching techniques in isolation — it's the transformation of content into representations, analogies, and explanations tailored to what makes a topic hard for students.
points: Shulman diagnoses a “missing paradigm” in teacher-effectiveness research: subject matter content had been stripped out in favor of generic, content-free pedagogical competencies.

Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) — the blend of subject expertise and teachability, including analogies, representations, and awareness of common student misconceptions — is framed as the most crucial, distinctively teacherly form of knowledge.
Case knowledge (specific, documented episodes) functions as prototypes, precedents, and parables, serving as a necessary complement to abstract propositional knowledge like principles and maxims.

“Strategic knowledge” — professional judgment exercised when principles collide, like maintaining pace versus extending wait-time — is what separates skilled improvisation from simply following a rulebook, but the field lacks a robust shared case literature to teach it explicitly.
quotes: Shulman begins by confronting the historical slight against teachers, arguing that the profession has been plagued by the notion that those who cannot perform simply teach, contrasting this view with an earlier Aristotelian perspective where teaching was considered the ultimate demonstration of knowledge.
The ultimate test of understanding rests on the ability to transform one's knowledge into teaching.

Teachers need an "armamentarium" of powerful representations, including analogies, illustrations, examples, explanations, and demonstrations, specifically tailored to make topics comprehensible to students.
Cases act as prototypes (exemplifying principles), precedents (capturing wisdom of practice), and parables (conveying norms and values).
Principles (propositions) are often decontextualized and may collide in practice (e.g., wait-time vs. pace), limiting their utility.
